passages.happening:
Matthew begins his book with a family tree. The first line is a title for what follows: “This is the record of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (verse 1). Then come the names, father to son, from Abraham down to King David.

Most of the names are men. But four times Matthew does something unusual and names a mother. Tamar (verse 3). Rahab (verse 5). Ruth (verse 5). And a woman he does not name at all, only “Uriah’s wife” (verse 6), who was Bathsheba.

Christ is not Jesus' surname. It is a title. It is the Greek form of the Hebrew word Messiah, which means ‘anointed one’: the king God had promised to send.
passages.hearers:
To us a list of names is the page we skip. To a first-century Jew it was the opposite. Your family line said who you were. Priests had to be able to prove their descent before they could serve (Ezra 2:61-63). A claim to be a king's heir was only as good as your family tree.

So the title is a bold claim. ‘Son of David’ meant heir to Israel's royal house, the line God promised would rule forever (2 Samuel 7:12-16). ‘Son of Abraham’ went further back, to the man God promised that “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3). Jesus belongs to Israel's king and to a promise meant for the whole world.

Readers of the Greek Old Testament would also notice the first words. In Greek, verse 1 begins biblos geneseōs, ‘the book of the genesis’. The Greek Old Testament uses that phrase in only two places, both in Genesis (2:4 and 5:1). Some scholars think Matthew is hinting at a new beginning, as if a new Genesis starts here. Others think he simply means ‘family record’. Both readings are held.

Then the women. Ancient family trees rarely named women at all, so these four stand out. Each had a story people remembered. Tamar dressed as a prostitute to get justice from her father-in-law Judah (Genesis 38). Rahab was a Canaanite who hid Israel's spies in Jericho (Joshua 2). Ruth was from Moab, a nation Israel had long been at odds with (Ruth 1:4). Bathsheba was taken by David while her husband Uriah, a Hittite, was at war (2 Samuel 11). Outsiders and scandal, right in the king's line.
passages.ot: The whole list is a short walk through the Old Testament. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob are the fathers of Israel in Genesis. Judah is the son whose line would carry the ruler's staff (Genesis 49:10). Boaz and Ruth are the great-grandparents of David (Ruth 4:17-22). And David is the king who received God's promise of a son whose throne would last forever (2 Samuel 7:16). By the time a hearer reaches David the king in verse 6, the story is pointing forward.
passages.hard: Why would Matthew include women with such stories? Readers have offered more than one answer. Some note that several were outsiders: Rahab a Canaanite, Ruth a Moabite, Bathsheba the wife of a Hittite, and Tamar perhaps one too. If so, the list hints from its first lines that this Messiah is for the nations. Others note that each woman's marriage or pregnancy was unusual and talked about. That prepares the reader for Mary, whose pregnancy would also cause whispers, though it came from God. Many think both are true. What the list does not do is hide anything. Israel's greatest king came from a family with stories nobody would invent to impress.
passages.asks: Matthew could have tidied up Jesus' family tree. He chose to leave in the outsiders and the scandals. What does that say about the kind of people God works through? If you think your own story disqualifies you from God's purposes, read verses 3 to 6 again.

passages.t: From David, through the exile, to the Messiah
passages.happening:
The list goes on from David through the kings who ruled in Jerusalem, Solomon, Rehoboam and the rest, down to Josiah and Jeconiah ‘at the time of the exile to Babylon’ (verse 11). Then come names after the exile, most of them unknown to us, down to Joseph, “the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ” (verse 16).

Notice how verse 16 changes the pattern. Every line before it says ‘was the father of’. This line does not say Joseph was the father of Jesus. It says Jesus was born of Mary. Matthew is already preparing for the story that follows.

Verse 17 sums it up in three groups of fourteen: Abraham to David, David to the exile, the exile to the Christ.
passages.hearers:
Three moments mark the list: Abraham, David and the exile. A Jewish hearer would feel the shape. Abraham was the promise. David was the high point, when Israel had its king. The exile was the low point. In 587 or 586 BC the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem and its temple and carried its people away (2 Kings 25). After that, no son of David sat on a throne again.

So the list tells Israel's story as a rise, a fall, and a long wait. The third group, the names after the exile, are quiet people nobody wrote about. Then the wait ends with the Christ. Matthew is saying that the story that seemed to stop at Babylon has reached its goal.

Why fourteen? Hebrew letters also stand for numbers. David's name in Hebrew is written with three letters, d-w-d, and their values add up to fourteen. Many scholars think that is Matthew's point: this whole family tree has David's number stamped on it.
passages.hard:
Two problems are worth facing.

First, Matthew leaves names out. Between Joram and Uzziah (verse 8) he skips three kings that 1 Chronicles 3:11-12 lists. And if you count the last group, you find thirteen names, not fourteen, unless someone is counted twice. Matthew's readers had the same Scriptures and could check. The list is shaped to teach, not to record every link, and the pattern matters more to him than completeness.

Second, Luke gives a different family tree (Luke 3:23-38). From David, Luke's line runs through Nathan, not Solomon, and it names Joseph's father as Heli, not Jacob. Christians have explained this in several ways: that one list follows a legal father and one a natural father, through the old custom of a brother marrying a dead brother's widow (Deuteronomy 25:5-6; this was the answer of Julius Africanus in the early 200s); that Luke traces Mary's line; or that Matthew traces the royal right to the throne and Luke the actual descent. Many scholars think the two lists came from different family traditions and cannot be fully joined. The site does not choose among these.

There is also Jeconiah (verse 11). Jeremiah said that none of his descendants would sit on David's throne (Jeremiah 22:30). Some answer that Jesus was Joseph's legal son, not his natural one. Others point out that God later called Jeconiah's grandson Zerubbabel “My signet ring” (Haggai 2:23), as if the judgment had been turned back.
passages.asks: The list covers about two thousand years, and in the last part nothing seems to happen. Names, and nothing more. Yet Matthew says God was steering all of it. When your own life feels like a stretch of names with no story, what would it mean to trust that the story has not stopped?

passages.t: Mary is with child, and Joseph's choice
passages.happening:
Mary is pledged to marry Joseph. Before they live together, she is found to be pregnant “through the Holy Spirit” (verse 18). Joseph knows the child is not his. He is a righteous man, and he does not want to shame her in public, so he decides to end the marriage quietly.

Then an angel speaks to him in a dream. Do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife, the angel says. The child is from the Holy Spirit. And Joseph is to name him Jesus, “because He will save His people from their sins” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
A Jewish marriage in this time came in two stages. First the betrothal, a binding promise made before witnesses. From then on the couple were treated as husband and wife, though they did not yet live together. Later came the wedding, when the husband brought his bride home. That is why Matthew calls Joseph ‘her husband’ (verse 19) and speaks of divorce, though they were not yet living together. Jewish law, as later written down in the Mishnah (Kiddushin 1:1), says such a woman was freed only by divorce or by her husband's death.

So Mary's pregnancy was serious. Under the law of Moses a betrothed woman who slept with another man could face death (Deuteronomy 22:23-24). Joseph could have accused her in public. Instead he chooses the quietest way out the law allowed. Matthew calls that righteous: faithful to God's law, and merciful in how he kept it.

The name mattered. Jesus is the Greek form of the Hebrew Yeshua, a shorter form of Joshua, which means ‘the LORD saves’. It was a common name; the Jewish historian Josephus mentions a number of men called Jesus. But the angel explains it: this child will do what his name says. And by naming him, Joseph takes him as his own son, into David's family.

Hearers might also catch an echo. Another Joseph, whose father was Jacob, dreamed dreams and went down to Egypt (Genesis 37 to 50). Matthew's Joseph, son of Jacob (verse 16), will do the same.
passages.ot: ‘He will save His people from their sins’ echoes the hope of Psalm 130:8, that God “will redeem Israel from all iniquity.” Israel had hoped for many kinds of rescue: from Rome, from poverty, from exile. The angel names the deepest one first.
passages.hard: Is the virgin conception history or legend? Matthew and Luke tell it independently, from different sides: Matthew from Joseph's, Luke from Mary's (Luke 1:26-38). Neither tells it as a myth about gods; both tell it soberly, with a frightened young couple and a scandal to manage. Skeptics answer that miracle stories are not the kind of thing history can confirm, and that birth stories grew up around great men in the ancient world. Christians answer that if God is the Creator, a new beginning in a human womb is not beyond him, and that the creeds confess Jesus ‘born of the Virgin Mary’ because Matthew and Luke both report it. A reader can weigh this honestly. The claim is that God himself began something new.
passages.asks: Joseph had every right to protect his name. He chose mercy before he knew the whole story, and obedience once he did. Is there someone you are entitled to shame, and could choose to spare? And when God's call costs you your reputation, as it cost Joseph his, will you still take Mary home?

passages.happening:
Matthew stops the story to explain it. All this happened, he says, to fulfil what the Lord said through the prophet: “Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and they will call Him Immanuel” (which means, “God with us”) (verse 23).

Then the story finishes simply. Joseph wakes up and does what the angel said. He takes Mary home as his wife. He has no union with her until the child is born. And he names the boy Jesus.
passages.hearers:
This is the first of about ten times Matthew says something happened ‘to fulfil’ what a prophet said. A Jewish hearer would know at once where the words come from: Isaiah 7. They would also know the setting there. Around 735 BC, two kings were marching against Jerusalem, and King Ahaz was terrified. Isaiah offered him a sign: a child would be born, and before the child was old enough to know right from wrong, the two kings' lands would be laid waste (Isaiah 7:16).

So the first hearers of Isaiah expected a child in their own day. Matthew sees something more in the words. The name in the prophecy, Immanuel, says that God is with his people. Matthew says that in Jesus, it is true in the fullest way: not only that God is on our side, but that God has come to be with us.
passages.ot: Isaiah's ‘God with us’ runs through his whole book of that time. The same phrase rings out as a defiant hope in Isaiah 8:10, “For God is with us.” And a little later Isaiah promises a child on David's throne who will be called “Mighty God” (Isaiah 9:6). Matthew reads Isaiah 7 in the light of those chapters around it.
passages.hard:
Two questions are often asked here.

The first is the word ‘virgin’. Isaiah's Hebrew word is almah, a young woman of age to marry. Most scholars today say it does not by itself mean ‘virgin’, and many English Bibles translate Isaiah 7:14 ‘young woman’. The Greek translation of Isaiah, made by Jews before Jesus' time, used parthenos, the usual Greek word for a virgin, and Matthew quotes the Greek. Many Jewish readers hold that Isaiah meant a child of Ahaz's day, and that Matthew reads more into the verse than Isaiah meant. Some Christians hold that Isaiah looked straight ahead to Jesus. Many others hold that the sign had a first meaning in Ahaz's day and a fuller meaning in Jesus. The belief that Jesus was born of a virgin does not rest on one Hebrew word; it rests on what Matthew and Luke both tell.

The second is the word ‘until’ in verse 25. Did Mary and Joseph have other children later? Catholic and Orthodox Christians hold that Mary remained a virgin all her life, and read Jesus' ‘brothers’ (13:55) as cousins or as Joseph's children by an earlier marriage. Many Protestants read them as younger children of Mary and Joseph. The word ‘until’ does not settle it either way; it says only what was true before the birth. Christians on both sides agree on what Matthew is stressing: Jesus was not Joseph's son by nature.
passages.asks: Matthew's book begins with ‘God with us’ (1:23) and ends with Jesus saying “I am with you always” (28:20). Where do you most need to hear that God is with you, not only for you? And if he is with you, what fear could you put down today?
